title: What is the Civil Air Patrol?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Civil Air Patrol, a nonprofit civilian auxiliary under the U.S. Air Force. They cover its origins in the late 1930s as civilian aviators offered help before U.S. entry into World War Two, its founding under Fiorello LaGuardia and Gil Robb Wilson on December 1, 1941, its coastal anti-submarine patrols against German U-boats (including the claimed but disputed bombings), its wartime duties such as target-glider towing and wolf culling in Texas, postwar search and rescue, the cadet and senior programs, drone escort and counterdrug work, and its membership and funding today. The episode also includes a stat-based ad break, a brief tangent on the Brits' accent and the origin of the mullet, and a listener mail segment about fluency and dreaming in a second language.

segments.title: What the Civil Air Patrol is
segments.summary: Overview of the Civil Air Patrol as a nonprofit civilian group under U.S. Air Force control, with quasi-military hierarchy, search and rescue work, the cadet program, and its link to Air Force enlistment and rank benefits.

segments.title: Accent tangent
segments.summary: Brief tangent on the British accent, saying the British originally sounded American and the BBC later adopted an Oxford-style accent.

segments.title: Origins in interwar civilian aviation
segments.summary: Private flying grew in the 1920s and 1930s. When European fascist governments shut down civilian flying, American civilian aviators organized to offer their services to the military. Gil Robb Wilson and Milton Knight are credited with founding civilian auxiliary programs.

segments.title: Founding under LaGuardia and Pearl Harbor
segments.summary: Wilson developed a plan and got support from Fiorello LaGuardia. The Civil Air Patrol was established December 1, 1941, six days before the attack on Pearl Harbor. Initially it was part of the U.S. Army Air Corps and its emblem was described.

segments.title: Coastal patrol against U-boats
segments.summary: German U-boats attacked U.S. coastal shipping early in the war. The Civil Air Patrol flew coastal patrols, and the hosts describe how the presence of a plane made submarines dive. A Cape Canaveral sandbar incident is described, and Hap Arnold authorized bombs and depth charges for CAP planes. The hosts note that official records of sinkings are disputed.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the statistics on the coastal patrol are discussed.

segments.title: Coastal patrol statistics and casualties
segments.summary: Stats on the coastal patrol: 173 subs spotted, 82 depth-charge attacks, 17 mines found, 363 people rescued. The coastal patrol lasted about eighteen months. Pilots flew about 500,000 hours, were paid eight dollars a day, and 26 to 30 pilots died. In 2014 Obama posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor to CAP members. A barbershop mullet anecdote follows.

segments.title: Other wartime missions
segments.summary: Besides coastal patrol, CAP ferried supplies and people, towed target gliders for anti-aircraft gunnery, and was tasked with culling wolves in Texas to protect cattle herds.

segments.title: Postwar status and search and rescue
segments.summary: After World War Two, the Army Air Corps became the Air Force. A law established CAP but barred arming it. CAP was later placed in the Air Combat Command. Search and rescue became its best-known role, including after the 1964 Alaska earthquake, and it now uses cell phone forensic teams.

segments.title: Membership, dues and today's fleet
segments.summary: Today CAP is all-volunteer, members pay dues and buy their own uniforms, and the Air Force covers expenses on missions. CAP has about 530 single-engine planes and more than 4,000 planes used yearly. It works with the Forestry Service and DEA, including counterdrug aerial surveillance, and provides drone escorts and training routes surveys for the military.

segments.title: Cadet and senior ranks, flight training
segments.summary: Cadets can join under eighteen, and those who join earlier can delay becoming seniors until twenty-one, which lets them get pilot training at about half price.

segments.title: Listener mail: fluency and dreaming in a second language
segments.summary: A Spanish teacher from Toledo, Ohio writes that the belief that you are fluent once you dream in a language is a myth and argues proficiency matters more than fluency. Josh and Chuck sign off with a University of Toledo Rockets shout-out.
